content:
Few phrases do more work in Christian argument than "the new covenant". It carries the claim that the first covenant was always meant to be replaced, and it answers the Muslim question whether a later revelation can stand beside an earlier one. It comes from one passage in the book of Jeremiah, and the passage is shorter and plainer than the arguments built on it.

This article reads the passage first, then the texts that quote it, then what the Quran says about covenants. It quotes the World English Bible for the Bible and Saheeh International for the Quran. It does not say which reading of Hebrews a Christian must hold. It says what each text says, where the readings divide, and where a fair reader should stop and say Allāhu aʿlam.

The words come in Jeremiah 31:31-34, inside the chapters about the return from exile. "Behold, the days come," says Yahweh, "that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah: not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers in the day that I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt; which covenant of mine they broke."[1]

Three things stand out. The parties are named: Israel and Judah, the two halves of the divided kingdom. No other nation is mentioned. The old covenant is the one made at the exodus. And the fault is placed on one side only: "which covenant of mine they broke". The passage does not say that the covenant was defective. It says that the people broke it.

Verdict: the passage promises a renewal to the people who broke the first covenant. Whatever it means for others has to be argued from other texts, because this one does not say it.

Here is what is new. "I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people." The word is my law, torah in the Hebrew. The promise is about where the law will be written. It does not name another law.[2]

Other prophets say the same. Ezekiel 36:26-27 has God take away "the stony heart" and give "a heart of flesh", and "cause you to walk in my statutes. You will keep my ordinances and do them." The Torah itself had already promised this: "Yahweh your God will circumcise your heart ... to love Yahweh your God with all your heart" (Deuteronomy 30:6).[3] Obedience from the inside was a hope inside the old covenant, long before Jeremiah.

Verdict: the newness is in the place of the law and the ease of keeping it, and the content is the same. A reader who finds in Jeremiah a cancelled law is reading something into it.

The forgiveness in the passage is direct. "I will forgive their iniquity, and I will remember their sin no more." There is no priest, no offering and no mediator in it. The only teaching that ends is the reminder to a neighbour to "know Yahweh", because "they will all know me, from their least to their greatest".[4]

The verses that follow tie the covenant to creation. If the ordinances of the sun, the moon and the stars "depart from before me", then "the offspring of Israel also will cease from being a nation before me forever" (31:35-37). Jeremiah 32:40 calls it "an everlasting covenant".[5] The text expects Israel to continue, and Paul agrees in Romans 11:29: "the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable."[6]

Verdict: in Jeremiah the new covenant is forgiveness and an inward law, given to a people that lasts. It is not a transfer of the promise to another people.

The Torah itself treats a covenant as something each generation takes up again. Moses tells the second generation in the wilderness: "Yahweh our God made a covenant with us in Horeb. Yahweh didn't make this covenant with our fathers, but with us, even us, who are all of us here alive today" (Deuteronomy 5:2-3). In chapter 29 he adds that the covenant is made with those who stand there, "the foreigners who are in the middle of your camps", and "also with those who are not here with us today".[7]

The books of history show the pattern again and again. Joshua "made a covenant with the people that day" at Shechem and wrote it in the book of the law (Joshua 24:25-26). King Josiah read "all the words of the book of the covenant" to the people and "made a covenant before Yahweh, to walk after Yahweh, and to keep his commandments" (2 Kings 23:1-3), and in Nehemiah 9:38 the returned exiles say, "we make a sure covenant, and write it."[8] In each case the book stays and the people pledge themselves to it again.

That matters for the word new. Read against this background, Jeremiah's covenant can be the next and deepest renewal, one that does not fail because the law is inside. Hebrews gives the word a harder sense. The Hebrew Bible supplies the first reading and the Letter supplies the second, and the reader chooses between them.

Verdict: the Hebrew Bible already renews its covenant with each generation around the same book. The word new in Jeremiah can belong to that series.

The Letter to the Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 in full, in chapter 8, and draws a conclusion: "In that he says, 'A new covenant', he has made the first old. But that which is becoming old and grows aged is near to vanishing away" (8:13). In chapter 10 it adds that where sins are remitted, "there is no more offering for sin" (10:18).[9]

The argument turns on the word new. Hebrews also quotes the passage in its Greek form, which differs from the Hebrew in one clause: Hebrews has God say "I disregarded them" where the Hebrew text has "I was a husband to them".[10] The point is small, and it shows that the argument in Hebrews rests on a reading of the translation.

Christians who follow Hebrews take the old covenant to be fulfilled and the sacrifices to be ended by the death of Jesus. Luke 22:20 has the cup "the new covenant in my blood". Other Christians point to Matthew 5:17-19, "not even one smallest letter or one tiny pen stroke shall in any way pass away from the law", and to Romans 3:31, "we establish the law".[11] The articles on Paul and the law and on the fulfilment quotations in Matthew set out that debate.

Verdict: Hebrews says the first covenant is vanishing, and the texts it quotes say the law is written inside. Both readings are held inside Christianity, and the reader has to weigh them.

The Quran does not speak of one new covenant. It speaks of a covenant with the Children of Israel (2:40, 2:63, 5:12), a covenant with the Christians (5:14), a covenant with the prophets (3:81, 33:7) and a covenant with the believers (5:7).[12] The diagnosis in 5:13 resembles Jeremiah's: "for their breaking of the covenant We cursed them and made their hearts hardened." The fault was in the people.

The remedy differs. In 3:81 God takes a covenant from the prophets that "whatever I give you of the Scripture and wisdom and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him." That is a covenant among prophets, renewed by each one and concluded by the last. The article on the covenant of the prophets sets it out, and the seal of the prophets says why Muslims hold the line to be closed.

The Quran also answers the point about forgiveness. "Do not despair of the mercy of Allāh. Indeed, Allāh forgives all sins" (39:53), and no intercessor acts "except after His permission" (10:3).[13] Forgiveness in the Quran needs repentance and God's mercy. It does not need a ransom, and the article on ransom compares the two.

Verdict: the diagnosis is shared, and the remedies are three: God writes the law inside, a death ends the offerings, a final messenger confirms the earlier ones. The word covenant is the same in all of them and the structure is not.

The bottom line

On the question put in the debate, whether the Quran can speak of a covenant too, the answer is yes, and it speaks of many. But a covenant that renews and a covenant that replaces are different ideas, and the texts say which one each tradition means. Jeremiah, read alone, is a renewal: the same law, written inside, forgiven without a sacrifice, to a people that remains. Hebrews reads it as a replacement. The Quran reads the line of covenants as a chain that one messenger confirms and closes.

Al-Fārūqī's method is useful here. It separates the revelation each prophet received from the history that gathered around it, and it faults the earlier communities for their historical form. Applied to covenants, the Quran blames what people did with the covenant and does not blame the covenant. Jeremiah does the same. On that point the Hebrew prophet and the Quran stand closer to each other than either stands to the theology of replacement, and a reader of any faith can check this against the verses quoted above.

The claim that decides the matter is not found in Jeremiah. It is found in what one believes about Jesus, and that is argued in its own article. A reader who wants the context of the question will find it in the nine questions from the floor. Allāhu aʿlam.

Notes

  1. Jeremiah 31:31-37, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  2. Jeremiah 31:33, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com); the Hebrew word is torah, as stated from general knowledge.
  3. Ezekiel 36:26-28 and Deuteronomy 30:6, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  4. Jeremiah 31:34, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  5. Jeremiah 31:35-37 and 32:38-40, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  6. Romans 11:26-29, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  7. Deuteronomy 5:2-3 and 29:10-15, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  8. Joshua 24:25-26, 2 Kings 23:1-3 and Nehemiah 9:38, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  9. Hebrews 8:6-13 and 10:15-18, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com).
  10. That Hebrews 8:9 follows the Greek (Septuagint) wording, "I disregarded them", where the Hebrew text of Jeremiah 31:32 has "I was a husband to them", is stated from general knowledge. The manuscripts and the standard commentaries were not opened for this article, and the World English Bible renders the Hebrew clause as "I was a husband to them".
  11. Luke 22:20, Matthew 5:17-19, Romans 3:31 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, read in the World English Bible (bible-api.com). That a few Western manuscripts, such as Codex Bezae, lack part of Luke 22:19-20 is stated from general knowledge and was not checked for this article.
  12. Quran 2:40, 2:63, 3:81, 5:7, 5:12-14, 7:169 and 33:7, Saheeh International, read on the Quran.com API.
  13. Quran 39:53, 10:3 and 53:26, Saheeh International, read on the Quran.com API.
